data.creedFields:
CREED: INQUISITIVE
Counters threats by studying
them, finding the pattern,
working the angle.

DRIVE: ATONEMENT
She believes she failed to stop
something dangerous once,
knowingly or not, and is trying
to settle that debt.

play.ambition: Build an airtight case  -  proof enough for herself  -  against the thing that walked out of her courtroom, and make sure it never happens to anyone else.
play.desire: Get through the next case without letting the system fail someone the way it failed her.
play.touchstones:
Open  -  still to be built out.
Candidates: a mentor in the DA’s
office who does not know why she
has changed; a defendant she
helped convict while distracted
by the real case; someone from
the original case still out
there, unaware of what almost
happened to them.
play.notes:
Best trait: Intelligence  -  the relentless,
detail-obsessed legal mind that missed nothing the
second time around.

TONE
Sharp, controlled, courtroom-composed even in
danger. She does not lose her cool; she redirects
it.

NOTE ON SKILLS
The source sheet lists Empathy 1 alongside Insight
2. Hunter 5e renamed Empathy to Insight, so the
higher value is used here.
play.history:
Vivienne Okafor is an Assistant District Attorney in New York, seven years in, sharp enough that she has stopped being surprised when opposing counsel recognises her name before she has said it. She built her reputation on being unshakeable  -  the kind of prosecutor who does not blink, does not rattle, closes strong. Then she lost a case she should have won.

The defendant walked. Clean acquittal, no technicality, just a jury that believed a story Vivienne knew was not true. She spent months afterward picking the trial apart, convinced she had missed something in the evidence or the witness prep. What she eventually found was not a legal error. It was a pattern of details she had dismissed as irrelevant  -  because they made no rational sense  -  that only made sense once she stopped assuming the defendant was human.

She never got to retry the case; double jeopardy saw to that. What she got instead was the absolute certainty that something walked out of her courtroom that should never have been found not guilty by any court, and that certainty has not left her. She still works the DA’s office by day. At night she is trying to make sure it does not happen again  -  and quietly hunting for a way to finish what the trial could not.
